Anomaly detection models normality and flags deviation, at the cost of threshold setting and false alarms [3]–[5]. Network intrusions are collective anomalies: a single flow from a scanner looks benign; the fan-out across a window does not [3].\n10: \n11: The closed-world critique applies directly: training and testing on the same capture with overlapping families and tuned thresholds reports memorisation, not detection [4]. Controls adopted here follow [4]: train on benign traffic only, hold out each attack family in turn, fix the alert unit before quoting any metric, and report bands over multiple seeds. Drift surveys add the second control: monitor score distributions, not labels, and recalibrate on flags rather than on schedule [6].\n12: \n13: ## 2.2 Datasets and flow features\n14: \n15: CICIDS2017 is the primary benchmark: five days, benign background plus seven attack families, ~2.8M flows [7]. Only the 85-column `GeneratedLabelledFlows` release (Flow ID, Source/Destination IP, Protocol, Timestamp, latin-1) can build host graphs; the 79-column `MachineLearningCSV` release has no IP columns and feeds per-flow models only [7]. CSE-CIC-IDS2018 repeats this pattern: 1 of 10 processed files is graph-usable and column names change a third time [8]. CTU-13 (13 botnet scenarios) and UNSW-NB15 (hybrid synthetic-plus-real, nine families) supply external replication [9], [10].\n16: \n17: Flow vocabulary follows CICFlowMeter: 80+ per-flow statistics over packet lengths, inter-arrival times, flags, and segment sizes [11]. Ports alone fail as keys once ephemeral randomisation appears [7], [11]. Two preprocessing constraints matter more than any architecture: (i) NaN-address rows (notably Thursday WebAttacks, ~63% unusable) must be dropped explicitly before host-set construction; (ii) byte/packet counts are power-law, so plain min-max lets a few busy hosts own the alert queue and log-compression before scaling is required.\n18: \n19: | Capture | Scale | Graph-usable |\n20: |---|---|---|\n21: | CICIDS2017 [7] | ~2.8M flows, 7 families | 85-col release only |\n22: | CSE-CIC-IDS2018 [8] | ~16M flows | 1 of 10 files |\n23: | CTU-13 [9] | 13 scenarios | Yes, with column map |\n24: | UNSW-NB15 [10] | ~2.5M flows, 9 families | Yes |\n25: \n26: ## 2.3 Reconstruction-based detection\n27: \n28: Isolation Forest (path length), one-class SVM (kernel boundary distance), and PCA (linear subspace residual) are the shallow references [12]–[14]. They capture global structure and miss nonlinear interactions between timing, flag, and volume features. Deterministic autoencoders (bottleneck reconstruction error) and variational autoencoders (latent-distribution deviation) beat them on network data while remaining per-flow [15], [16]. Stacked autoencoders on CICFlowMeter features confirmed the same pattern at larger scale [17]. The study represents enterprise authentication activity as a sequence of directed temporal graphs, with accounts or machines as nodes and authentication events as edges. The work also leaves the relationship between scalability, threshold calibration, and analyst workload insufficiently resolved. {"type":"tool","tool":"write","name":"write","id":"call_01a0c4bacaf471e7944010439554be75","args":{"filePath":"E:\\Potential-gold\\Zero-Day\\docs\\report\\ch2_v3\\ch2_part1.tex","content":"% ch2_part1 -- protocol (2.1) + datasets (2.2). Markers [1]-[9] = P01,P13,P14,P02,P28,P29,P36,P37,P38.\n% ASCII-safe LaTeX only. One marker per paper at paragraph start.\n\n\\section{Evaluation protocol}\n\nThis chapter reviews 40 distinct studies: protocol 3, datasets 6, reconstruction 4, graph 10, drift/adversarial/explain 15, UEBA 2. No duplicate merges were required in this register (the P12/P33 team-Excel merge is already recorded under \\cite{panchal2026}).\n\n\\textbf{[1] Closed world (2010) ---} Sommer and Paxson \\cite{sommer2010} argue that training and testing on the same capture with overlapping families reports memorisation, not detection. Controls adopted here follow them: benign-only training, held-out attack families, a fixed alert unit, and multi-seed bands.\n\n\\textbf{[2] Anomaly survey (2009) ---} Chandola et al.\\ \\cite{chandola2009} frame network intrusions as collective anomalies: one scanner flow looks benign, the fan-out across a window does not. This is the premise for host-window aggregation in Chapter~3.\n\n\\textbf{[3] IDS taxonomy (1999) ---} Debar et al.\\ \\cite{debar1999} separate signature systems (miss unseen families by definition) from anomaly systems (model normality, pay in thresholds and false alarms). The project is anomaly-side throughout.\n\n\\section{Datasets and flow features}\n\n\\textbf{[4] CICIDS2017 (2018) ---} Sharafaldin et al.\\ \\cite{sharafaldin2018} supply the primary benchmark: five days, benign background plus seven attack families, about 2.8M flows. Only the 85-column GeneratedLabelledFlows release (Flow ID, Source/Destination IP, Protocol, Timestamp, latin-1) can build host graphs; the 79-column MLCSV release has no IP columns and feeds per-flow models only.\n\n\\textbf{[5] LID-DS 2021 (2022) ---} Grimmer et al.\\ \\cite{grimmer2022} provide the future Pillar-3 host eval set (CRITIS 2022, LNCS 13723). The official baseline is STIDE; no benign-only Isolation Forest SOTA exists on LID-DS and none is quoted.\n\n\\textbf{[6] CERT r6.2 (2013) ---} Glasser and Lindauer \\cite{glasser2013} generate the CMU SEI insider-threat set (4000 users, 5 malicious; logon, device, http, email, file). It is the Pillar-2 UEBA reference, not NIDS data.\n\n\\textbf{[7] CTU-13 (2014) ---} Garcia et al.\\ \\cite{garcia2014} publish 13 botnet scenarios for external replication; infected hosts rank first in our CTU-13 runs.\n\n\\textbf{[8] UNSW-NB15 (2015) ---} Moustafa and Slay \\cite{moustafa2015} supply the hybrid synthetic-plus-real set (nine families) used as a second external check.\n\n\\textbf{[9] CICFlowMeter (2017) ---} Lashkari \\cite{lashkari2017} defines the flow vocabulary: 80+ per-flow statistics over packet lengths, inter-arrival times, flags, and segment sizes. A threshold tuned where it is measured borrows information from the test distribution: the operating point is chosen after seeing which attacks arrive, so the reported accuracy describes a detector that already knows the exam questions. The honest alternative fixes the threshold on benign validation plus a held-out attack slice, then freezes it before the test families are ever scored. That discipline costs headline points and buys transferability, which is the trade this project accepts throughout. Window sizing interacts with the same mechanism through the collective-anomaly framing of [3]: a sixty-second window maximises precision at one hundred because attacker neighbourhoods stand out against small benign populations, while eighteen-hundred-second windows raise mean area under the curve by smoothing benign behaviour at the price of diluting the attacker into a larger crowd. Neither window is universally correct; the choice is a metric trade stated explicitly, with sixty seconds as the default because the alert queue, not the curve, is the operational object. A wider bottleneck reconstructs more faithfully, which lowers benign error but also lowers attack error, since an autoencoder wide enough to pass its input through unchanged reconstructs attacks as faithfully as normal traffic. The project measured this directly: latent widths from two to twelve move the mean by three thousandths, and hidden widths from thirty-two to sixty-four move it by two ten-thousandths. Architecture does not matter here; the bottleneck is a guardrail against identity mapping, not a performance lever. Calibration, by contrast, moves everything: raw reconstruction distances span 0.038 to 0.122 while benign maxima sit near 0.278, so any fixed threshold in that band is arbitrary, and percentile mapping against a benign holdout converts incomparable error scales into comparable ranks. The ensemble study in [13] adds the third mechanism, disagreement across experts, which stabilises the percentiles rather than adding modelling ideas: the five-member checkpoint exists so that one unfortunate initialisation cannot set the queue. Compared on methodologies, capacity control ([12]), score calibration (the percentile rule) and ensemble stabilisation ([13]) address three different failure modes, memorisation, incomparability and seed luck, in that order; compared on reported performances, calibration is the only one of the three that moves headline numbers by tens of points rather than thousandths.","oldString":"That is the gap the next section fills: the host-graph detector keeps the reconstruction objective these studies validate and changes only the aggregation scope from flows to host neighbourhoods, which is why the baseline-versus-graph comparison in this project holds features, protocol and seeds fixed and varies nothing but structure."},"output":[{"type":"text","text":"Edit applied successfully."}]}

Sudden drift, a service migration overnight, invalidates absolute thresholds while preserving rank order, so percentile-calibrated detectors survive it and fixed-threshold ones flood. Gradual drift, a growing user base, moves both, and only a monitor watching the score distribution catches it before the queue composition has already changed. Recurring drift, weekday-weekend cycles, punishes any adaptation that forgets: a detector retrained on weekend traffic unlearns the weekday normal it will need on Monday. The continual-learning studies in [34] and [35] answer with complementary memory policies. Strategic selection with forgetting in [34] maintains a bounded exemplar set: incoming samples are scored for drifted patterns, representative ones are rehearsed, and outdated samples are discarded once significant drift trips, reporting state-of-the-art adaptability on NSL-KDD and UNSW-NB15 from an International Conference on Computer Communications 2025 paper with released code. Representation enhancement in [35] re-shapes features toward drift-invariant forms through a self-supervised stage followed by weakly-supervised tuning. Compared on problems, selection manages what is remembered while reshaping manages what is represented; compared on methodologies, both assume labelled drift confirmation that a benign-only deployment does not have, which is why this project currently fields only the detection head in its rolling monitors, with adaptation scheduled rather than claimed. The explanation method in [29] supplies the complementary per-alert account: additive feature attributions that decompose one host-window score into per-dimension contributions, so that a PortScan alert points at an out-degree spike and a flooding alert at an in-degree collapse. The attributions describe the model rather than the ground truth, and under feature correlation, where degree and byte counts move together, competing explainers diverge; the fooling study in [37] then shows the explainers themselves can be attacked through out-of-distribution scaffolding. Compared on problems, [36] asks whether explanations are faithful, [37] asks whether they survive attack, and [38] asks whether analysts can use them; compared on systems, all terminate in the same analyst-facing surface of ranked, readable reasons, which is exactly what the triage drawer in the dashboard consumes.","oldString":"Together [28] and [17] with the closed-world controls of [4] define the monitoring posture here: three score streams watched by rolling monitors, every alert carrying its attribution, and re-calibration governed by drift flags rather than by calendar."},"output":{"type":"tool.execution","message":"Could not find oldString in the file. This survey tries to provide a structured and comprehensive overview of the research on anomaly detection. We have grouped existing techniques into different categories based on the underlying approach adopted by each technique. For each category we have identified key as sumptions, which are used by the techniques to differentiate between normal and anomalous behavior. When applying a given technique to a particular domain, these assumptions can be used as guidelines to assess the effectiveness of the technique in that domain. For each category, we provide a basic anomaly detection technique, and then show how the different existing techniques in that category are variants of the basic technique. This template provides an easier and more succinct understanding of the techniques belonging to each category. We also provide a discussion on the computational complexity of the techniques since it is an important issue in real application domains. We hope that this survey will provide a better understanding of the different directions in which research has been done on this topic, and how techniques developed in one area can be applied in domains for which they were not intended to begin with. In addition to the network topology, the order of information flow is crucial to detect cyber-threats in a constantly evolving network. Majority of the existing technique uses static snapshot to learn from dynamic network. However, using static snapshots is not sufficient as it largely ignores highly granular temporal information and leads to information loss due to approximation of aggregation granularity. In this work, we propose PIKACHU, a sophisticated, unsupervised, temporal walk-based dynamic network embedding technique that can capture both network topology as well as highly granular temporal information. PIKACHU learns the appropriate and meaningful representation by preserving the temporal order of nodes. This is important information to detect Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) as temporal order helps to understand the lateral movement of the attacker. Experiments on two open-source datasets: LANL and OpTC datasets demonstrated the effectiveness in detecting network anomalies. PIKACHU achieves True Positive Rate (TPR) of 95.1% in LANL and 98.7% on OpTC dataset. Furthermore, in the LANL dataset, it achieves a 4.65% reduction in False Positive Rate (FPR) despite similar area under ROC curve (AUC). The dataset group establishes which releases can support relational modelling at all. The final group centres on drift adaptation, continual learning, timing and structural evasion, certification, explanation and user and entity behavior analytics studies, which supply the evaluation controls the present work adopts. # Paper 1: EULER — your first paper

**One-line:** unsupervised temporal-graph link prediction for catching lateral movement, designed to scale to enterprise log volumes by parallelising what everyone else ran serially.

## 1. The problem (why it exists)

Earlier temporal graph detectors stacked a GNN (spatial: *who talks to whom*) on an RNN (temporal: *in what order*), wired **serially** — the GNN at time *t* needed the RNN's output from *t−1*. That's an O(T) dependency chain: no multi-core, no GPU clusters. Enterprise networks emit tens of millions of authentication events per hour, so those models simply couldn't run at real scale. EULER's question: can you break that chain without losing accuracy?

## 2. How it works (the mechanism — learn this cold)

Enterprise logins become **discrete temporal graphs**: nodes = users/machines, directed edges = authentication events (NTLM/Kerberos), sliced into **30-minute snapshots** (δ = 30 min, experimentally optimal — short enough to catch bursty lateral moves, long enough to keep structure).

The distributed pipeline has four stages:
1. **Chunking** — timeline split into contiguous snapshot slices across workers.
2. **Parallel encoding** — each worker runs a *replicated* GNN (GCN, GraphSAGE, or GAT — model-agnostic) on its own snapshots, concurrently. This is the breakthrough: snapshot *t* doesn't wait for *t−1*.
3. **Sequential integration** — a leader process streams the spatial embeddings in order through **one GRU** into dynamic embeddings Z_t.
4. **Decoding + thresholding** — inner-product decoder Â = σ(Z_t Z_tᵀ); low predicted probability on a real connection = anomaly. Threshold τ from a held-out validation snapshot with cost parameter **λ = 0.6** (biased toward fewer false positives).

## 3. Results (exact numbers)

- **Facebook:** AUC 92.20%, AP 91.74% (+4% over complex SI-VGRNN) — proves simple decoupled design doesn't lose representation quality.
- **LANL (58 days, 45.8M events):** GCN-GRU detector — AUC **0.9912**, TPR 86.10%, FPR 0.5698%; SAGE-GRU predictor — AUC 0.9847.
- **Limits to admit in viva:** 0.57% FPR is still hundreds of daily alerts at enterprise scale; fixed slicing can't do continuous-time; vulnerable to injected normal-looking logins; threshold-vs-workload unresolved.

## 4. Its role in OUR project

EULER is the **temporal baseline our fused variant ablates against** (repo [61], Ch2 §2.4). We take its unsupervised discipline; we differ everywhere else — host graphs on CICIDS (not auth logs), held-out families, edge-level alerts, seed bands.

---

**Your turn.** Explain EULER back to me in ~5 sentences, as if I'm the examiner. Then I'll hit you with questions — first one ready: *"Your project also builds graphs over time windows. Why didn't you just use EULER?"*

# Paper 2: The GNN Systematic Review (Alshehri) — your second paper

**One-line:** a PRISMA-style map of 28 GNN-for-security studies that tells the field *what's been tried and what's missing* — our chapter uses it as the architecture shortlist, not as evidence anyone wins.

## 1. The problem
GNN-for-security papers were scattered across venues with inconsistent terms: GCN here, GAT there, different datasets, different metrics. Nobody could say which architecture suits which threat. The review's job: impose order — taxonomy by architecture × dataset × attack type × metric × limitation.

## 2. How it works (method)
Systematic search across major academic databases → **200 records screened → 28 primary studies** (2020–2025). No new model, no experiments — corpus filtering + gap tabulation. That last point matters: *everything it concludes is only as good as the 28 primaries*.

## 3. Findings (the three you'll be asked about)
- **GCN appears most frequently; GAT is used for dynamic, transaction-heavy settings** but costs more memory/parameters.
- Reported F1s look high across provenance, phishing, IoT-botnet tasks — **but they're incomparable** (different preprocessing, splits, label definitions, metrics). No common leaderboard exists. Say this sentence in viva; it's the review's whole warning.
- **Named gaps:** interpretability void, standardisation deficit, encrypted-payload blind spot, dataset monoculture, missing dynamics.

## 4. Limits (admit before asked)
Inherits reporting bias (failed systems don't publish); identifies gaps without experimentally testing any; conclusions are a *map*, not proof of superiority. Publication strength 7/10 *as a review*.

## 5. Role in OUR project
It justifies our architecture shortlist (why SAGE/GCN/anomaly framings were compared at all) and our audit posture — dataset monoculture is *its* wound, and our IDS2018/CTU-13 replication is the bandage. Cited repo [28], Ch2 §2.4.

---

**Your turn:** explain it back in ~5 sentences. Then my first question: *"If the review itself says headline scores are incomparable, why does your chapter cite any performance numbers from GNN papers at all?"*

### [505/735] assistant (opencode/muse-spark-1.3-contributor-free) 2026-09-26T09:02:16.494Z
Fair — let me rebuild it from the ground up.

# Paper 2, slower: what a systematic review actually *does*

Forget "AI for security" for a minute. Imagine 200 people each baked a cake, each with a different recipe, different oven, different judge scoring "tastiness" out of different totals. Someone publishes a review saying "cake 7 scored 98!" — meaningless, because cake 7's judge gave marks out of 200 and cake 3's judge only tasted the frosting.

That's the state of GNN-for-security literature the authors walked into. Their fix has three mechanical steps — this is what "PRISMA-oriented" means in practice:

1. **Search widely, with written rules.** Query the major academic databases with fixed keywords (graph neural network × intrusion/malware/phishing), so anyone could repeat the search and get the same pool. Result: ~200 candidate records.
2. **Filter by explicit criteria.** Drop duplicates, non-English, non-peer-reviewed, papers that merely mention GNNs without building a detector, etc. Result: **28 primary studies, 2020–2025**. The criteria are published — that's what makes it *systematic* rather than "papers I happened to read."
3. **Tabulate, don't average.** For each of the 28, record: architecture (GCN? GAT? hybrid?), domain (provenance? phishing? IoT botnet?), dataset, attack types, metric + score, stated limitation. Then look for *patterns across the table* instead of declaring a winner.

## What the table actually says (with teeth)

- **GCN shows up most.** Not because it's proven best — because it's oldest, simplest, and runs cheapest. Popularity ≠ superiority; in viva, never let anyone flip those.
- **GAT appears where graphs move fast** (transaction-heavy, dynamic settings) because attention weights let the model re-weight neighbours per snapshot — but attention is quadratic-ish in cost, so it buys adaptivity with memory and parameters. That's a *trade*, and you should state it as one.
- **The high F1s are real numbers from unreal comparisons.** Paper A reports F1 0.97 on a provenance dataset with its own split; Paper B reports 0.95 on IoT traffic with 5-fold CV. Both honest, jointly meaningless — different data, different splits, different label definitions. This is *why* our chapter refuses leaderboards and why the R+R paper ([23]) exists: same disease, one level up (re-running instead of re-tabulating).

## Why the gaps matter for YOUR viva

Each named gap maps to something in our project — learn these pairs, examiners love "gap → your answer" structure:

| Review's gap | Our answer |
|---|---|
| Dataset monoculture | IDS2018 + CTU-13 replication, not CICIDS-only |
| Missing dynamics | Time-windowed host graphs (with the honest negative: our LSTM fusion added nothing) |
| Interpretability void | SHAP per-alert attributions, robustness-checked |
| Standardisation deficit | Pinned columns, seeded bands, stated alert unit |
| Encrypted-payload blind spot | Metadata-only detection (we never look at payloads — like Vectra/Cisco ETA in industry) |

## The one attack to expect

*"Your review-of-reviews cites 28 papers you never read. How is that scholarship?"* — Answer: we cite it **for its taxonomy and gap inventory**, never for a primary result. Every performance claim in our chapter comes from a paper (or our own runs), not from Alshehri's table. A review is a map; we walked the terrain ourselves where it mattered.

### [514/735] assistant (opencode/muse-spark-1.3-contributor-free) 2026-09-26T09:20:46.132Z
No shame in that — this is the most technical question so far. Let's build it piece by piece, then you'll answer it yourself.

## The whole argument in one picture

Imagine two hosts in the same window:

- **Scanner:** talks to **200** different machines (one probe each)
- **Normal laptop:** talks to **3** machines (mail, intranet, update server)

The *number itself* — 200 vs 3 — **is** the attack signal. Everything hinges on whether your math preserves that number or erases it.

## What each model does with those numbers

**GCN (Kipf):** when it builds host A's embedding, it *divides* each neighbour's contribution by the degrees of both endpoints — "symmetric normalisation." Think of it as grading on a curve *per neighbourhood*: the scanner's 200 tiny contributions each get shrunk, the laptop's 3 get boosted. After normalisation, both hosts look... similar-ish. The curve erased the evidence. That's perfect for citation graphs (a prolific author shouldn't dominate) and fatal for intrusion graphs (the fan-out count *is* the crime).

**GraphSAGE (Hamilton):** takes the *mean* of neighbour features — no degree-based shrinking. 200 neighbours still shout louder than 3. The count survives into the embedding, and the autoencoder downstream sees an anomalous neighbourhood for what it is.

## The inductive bonus (second half of the answer)

GCN in its classic form is **transductive**: embeddings are learned per node, so a host that appears next window needs retraining. New hosts arrive *every window* in our data. GraphSAGE is **inductive**: it learns an *aggregation function*, not per-node vectors — unseen nodes embed immediately. So SAGE wins twice: it keeps degree, and it handles new hosts for free.

## Your viva sentence

> "The choice is mechanistic, not fashionable. Symmetric normalisation divides away degree, and in intrusion graphs degree is the attack — one-to-many scan, many-to-one flood. Mean aggregation preserves it. Plus SAGE is inductive, so new hosts each window embed without retraining. We chose the operator whose math keeps our signal."

Now you: answer Q2 in your own words, including the 200-vs-3 example.

# Paper 3: XAI-IDR (Panchal) — Avinash's paper, but you must defend it too

**One-line:** a hybrid detector (1D CNN–LSTM + XGBoost/Random Forest) with SHAP/LIME explanations gating automated response — *contain only when confident AND explainable, else escalate to a human.*

## 1. The problem
High-accuracy IDS models are black boxes. Auto-containment on a black-box alert is dangerous (block the wrong port → outage), but manual review of every alert bottlenecks the SOC. Question: can explanations make *automated response safe*?

## 2. How it works
- **Detection:** 1D CNN–LSTM branch plus tree ensembles, evaluated on NSL-KDD, CIC-IDS2017/2018, IoT Botnet — F1/AUC in the high range.
- **Explanation:** SHAP + LIME + attention, local and global.
- **The contribution (learn this): the dual gate** — automatic containment triggers *only when prediction confidence AND explanation stability both exceed thresholds*; ambiguous cases escalate to a human. Safety from two keys, not one.

## 3. Limits (from our own nine-paper review — admit freely)
Real-time explanation latency unquantified, explanation-poisoning evaluated qualitatively not experimentally, **no MITRE mapping, no drift handling**, high benchmark scores ≠ production readiness, no ablations (which component actually helps?).

## 4. Role in OUR project
The dual-gate policy is the template for safe automation thinking; our ATT&CK mapper + triage drawer follow the post-hoc pattern. And [37] is where Slack [73] bites: explanations are attackable, so our explainer gets robustness-checked, never trusted blindly.

### [520/735] assistant (opencode/muse-spark-1.3-contributor-free) 2026-09-26T09:49:08.738Z
Alright, slower and concrete — let's start from the SOC floor, not the paper.

# Paper 3, rebuilt: why explanation gates action

## The scene (make this vivid — examiners remember stories)

It's 3 AM. Your detector fires: *"Host 10.4.2.19 is malicious, confidence 0.94."* Two options:

- **Act now:** auto-quarantine the host. If it's the file server, you've just taken the company offline over a false positive. Career-limiting.
- **Wait for a human:** page the analyst, who spends 40 minutes digging through flows to decide. Meanwhile the real attack spreads. Also bad.

This is the dilemma XAI-IDR attacks: **accuracy without justification is unactionable.** A score tells you *how sure*; it never tells you *why*. And "why" is what makes action safe.

## The three moving parts (separate them cleanly)

**1. The detector (hybrid — know why hybrid).**
A 1D CNN–LSTM branch reads *sequences* (packet/flow order matters — a scan has rhythm), while XGBoost + Random Forest read *tabular features* (counts, sizes, flags). Neither sees what the other sees, so they complement rather than duplicate. High F1/AUC on NSL-KDD, CIC-IDS2017/2018, IoT Botnet. Fine — but lots of papers have high F1. The detector is not the contribution.

**2. The explanations (three lenses, different jobs).**
- **SHAP:** for *this* alert, which features pushed the score up or down, and by how much (additive attributions — they sum to the score, so nothing hides).
- **LIME:** a cheap local approximation — "near this alert, the model behaves like *this simple rule*." Faster, rougher.
- **Attention:** the deep branch's own spotlight — which timesteps it stared at.
Local (this alert) *and* global (what the model cares about overall). The point: the analyst gets *ranked reasons*, not a bare number.

**3. The dual gate (THE contribution — slow down here).**
Two keys must turn together before anything automatic happens:

- **Key 1 — prediction confidence:** is the score far from the boundary, not a coin-flip 0.51?
- **Key 2 — explanation stability:** perturb the input slightly — do the *same* features still explain it? If the reasons flip under tiny noise, the explanation is fragile, and acting on it is gambling.

| | Stable explanation | Unstable explanation |
|---|---|---|
| **Confident** | ✅ auto-contain | 🙋 escalate to human |
| **Uncertain** | 🙋 escalate to human | 🙋 escalate to human |

Only one cell acts alone. Everything else pages a person. *That table* is what you're defending — draw it mentally in viva if asked.

## Why each stated limit actually matters (don't just list them — weaponize them)

- **Latency unquantified:** SHAP per alert costs real milliseconds. At 10k flows/sec, "per-alert explanation" can mean a queue that never drains. Our project answers with ranked top-k features only — bounded cost.
- **Poisoning only qualitative:** Slack [37] shows attackers can *craft inputs whose explanations lie* while the prediction stays wrong-but-confident. A dual gate whose second key can be forged is a locked door with the key under the mat — which is why our explainer gets robustness-checked.
- **No MITRE mapping:** reasons without tactic names ("out-degree spike" vs "reconnaissance") still make the analyst translate. Our ATT&CK mapper closes exactly this.
- **No drift, no ablations:** is it the CNN, the trees, or the gate doing the work? Unknown. Never claim more than "promising policy, environment-sensitive."

## Its role in OUR project, in one breath

XAI-IDR is the *policy* paper: confidence-plus-stability gating as the shape of safe automation. We bank the policy idea, implement the mapping it lacks, and distrust the explanations exactly as far as Slack says to.

---

### [536/735] assistant (opencode/muse-spark-1.3-contributor-free) 2026-09-26T10:29:30.214Z
# Paper 9 (your 3rd): R+R — "From Claims to Crashes"

**One-line:** an independent audit that re-ran five famous graph detectors and watched the published numbers fall apart — the reason our chapter trusts *protocols*, not headlines.

## 1. The problem
GNN security papers reported flawless metrics but hid their preprocessing pipelines and exact settings. "Performance inflation": brilliant on paper, collapsing when an enterprise team re-implements from scratch. Nobody had stress-tested the claims side by side.

## 2. How it works (the audit machine)
Standardized pipeline (**GidsRep**): raw logs (LANL, OpTC, CICIDS2017 + a fresh enterprise capture) normalized into flat graph inputs, five detectors run side by side — **EULER, ARGUS, Anomal-E, PIKACHU, VGRNN**. Five explicit research questions: which hyperparameters move results most? Do published numbers reproduce? Do systems generalize to fresh enterprise data? Where do they run out of memory? How easily are they evaded?

## 3. Findings (three numbers to memorize)
- **Replication deviates substantially** with metric/preprocessing/hyperparameter choices — same model, different pipeline, different headline.
- **Collapse on CICIDS2017 + enterprise data** with high false-positive rates — public-capture leaders fail where backgrounds differ.
- **2 adversarial edges cover all LANL attacks** (10 on OpTC) — evasion is *cheap* against these systems, which is why evasion must be priced, not assumed away.

Note the venue trail (examiner bait): arXiv March 2025 as *"Are We There Yet?"* → camera-ready *"R+R: From Claims to Crashes"* at **ACSAC 2025, Honolulu**. Cite the camera-ready title via arXiv:2503.20281; per-paper DOI pending, never invent one.

## 4. Role in OUR project
This paper is the *caution behind everything structural* in our work: seed bands (replication wobbles), pinned columns (preprocessing decides results), IDS2018/CTU-13 replication (single-capture numbers don't transfer), and the harness reporting attacker *cost* (because 2 edges can erase a detector).

---

Explain it back — then: *"R+R shows graph detectors collapse outside their home captures. Doesn't that result indict YOUR graph detector too?"*

# Paper 9 (your 3rd): R+R — "From Claims to Crashes" (regenerated)

**One-line:** an independent audit that re-ran five famous graph detectors and watched the published numbers fall apart — the reason our chapter trusts *protocols*, not headlines.

## 1. The problem
GNN security papers reported flawless metrics but hid their preprocessing pipelines and exact settings. "Performance inflation": brilliant on paper, collapsing when an enterprise team re-implements from scratch. Nobody had stress-tested the claims side by side.

## 2. How it works (the audit machine)
Standardized pipeline (**GidsRep**): raw logs (LANL, OpTC, CICIDS2017 + a fresh enterprise capture) normalized into flat graph inputs, five detectors run side by side — **EULER, ARGUS, Anomal-E, PIKACHU, VGRNN**. Five explicit research questions: which hyperparameters move results most? Do published numbers reproduce? Do systems generalize to fresh enterprise data? Where do they run out of memory? How easily are they evaded?

## 3. Findings (three numbers to memorize)
- **Replication deviates substantially** with metric/preprocessing/hyperparameter choices — same model, different pipeline, different headline.
- **Collapse on CICIDS2017 + enterprise data** with high false-positive rates — public-capture leaders fail where backgrounds differ.
- **2 adversarial edges cover all LANL attacks** (10 on OpTC) — evasion is *cheap* against these systems, which is why evasion must be priced, not assumed away.

Venue trail (examiner bait): arXiv March 2025 as *"Are We There Yet?"* → camera-ready *"R+R: From Claims to Crashes"* at **ACSAC 2025, Honolulu**. Cite the camera-ready title via arXiv:2503.20281; per-paper DOI pending, never invent one.

## 4. Role in OUR project
This paper is the *caution behind everything structural* in our work: seed bands (replication wobbles), pinned columns (preprocessing decides results), IDS2018/CTU-13 replication (single-capture numbers don't transfer), and the harness reporting attacker *cost* (because 2 edges can erase a detector).

---

Explain it back — then: *"R+R shows graph detectors collapse outside their home captures. Doesn't that result indict YOUR graph detector too?"*

Noted on both counts — and when those experiments merge, we'll walk the code and results line by line, viva-style, same as the papers. No shallow prompting.

# Paper 5: PIKACHU — Temporal-Walk Dynamic Graph Embedding

**One-line:** unsupervised embeddings that learn *the order nodes are visited*, built for catching lateral movement on provenance graphs — the closest published cousin to EULER, trading throughput for temporal fidelity.

## 1. The problem
Static snapshots aggregate a whole window into one graph, which destroys *order*: host A→B→C (lateral spread) and C→B→A (normal admin rounds) can look identical once timestamps are binned. For advanced persistent threats, order is the trail — the attacker creeps machine to machine over days. PIKACHU's question: can embeddings preserve visit order instead of collapsing it?

## 2. How it works (mechanism)
**Temporal walks, not snapshots.** Instead of cutting time into bins, it samples walks that respect event order — the walker can only step to edges that happened *after* the current one. Short-term embeddings are built from these continuous-time walks, so an ordered lateral path scores differently from the same edges in random order. Unsupervised throughout: no attack labels, just normal-visit structure learned from DARPA OpTC and LANL provenance captures.

## 3. Results (exact, correctly labelled)
**True-positive rates: 95.1% LANL / 98.7% OpTC** (doi 10.1109/NOMS54207.2022.9789921), 4.65% false-positive reduction on LANL at similar curve, 16% area improvement on OpTC. Say it exactly so: *detection rates on labelled captures — not recall, not held-out.* That's the correction we made in the chapter, and examiners probe it.

## 4. Limits
Paywalled evaluation (we cite the abstract, honestly flagged); provenance-only scope; no held-out-family protocol; data-hungry on ordered examples.

## 5. Role in OUR project
The walk-order idea sits between EULER (parallel snapshots, throughput) and us (windowed host graphs: order aggregated *inside* a window, preserved *across* windows). Cited repo [19]/local [16], Ch2 §2.4.

### [730/735] assistant (opencode/muse-spark-1.3-contributor-free) 2026-09-29T09:41:46.472Z
# Paper 5 (again, clearer): PIKACHU — learning the *order* of visits

## The problem, in plain words

Older systems cut time into buckets — everything in a 30-minute window becomes one static picture. But bucketing destroys **sequence**. Consider two cases with the same three machines:

- **Attack:** A → B → C (intruder hopping outward, day after day)
- **Normal:** C → B → A (admin doing rounds in reverse)

Same machines, same connections, opposite order. A snapshot sees both as one identical triangle and calls them the same. For advanced persistent threats — attackers who creep one machine per day — order is the *entire* trail. PIKACHU's question: what if embeddings remembered the order of visits instead of throwing it away?

## How it works, step by step

1. **No buckets.** The system reads the raw stream of provenance events (who touched what, when) from DARPA OpTC and LANL captures.
2. **Time-respecting walks.** It sends imaginary walkers across the graph with one strict rule: each step must go to an event that happened *after* the current one. A walker can follow A→B→C only if B happened after A — it can never walk backwards in time.
3. **Learning from walks.** Hosts that appear in similar ordered contexts get similar embeddings. Normal admin rounds form one pattern; slow lateral spread forms another. No attack labels anywhere — purely unsupervised.
4. **Scoring.** A new walk that doesn't fit learned normal orderings flags as anomalous.

The key contrast with EULER: EULER parallelises *snapshots* (fast, coarse — order inside a bucket is lost); PIKACHU preserves *order* (precise, slower, hungry for ordered examples). Throughput versus fidelity — pick your sacrifice.

## Results, labelled correctly

**True-positive rates: 95.1% on LANL, 98.7% on OpTC** — plus 4.65% fewer false positives on LANL and 16% better area on OpTC versus compared methods (doi 10.1109/NOMS54207.2022.9789921). These are *detection rates on labelled attack replays*, not recall under held-out families. That one sentence is worth marks; it's the correction we fought for in the chapter.

## Limits, stated plainly

Needs lots of ordered examples to learn from; the evaluation paper sits behind a paywall (we cite the published abstract, flagged honestly); provenance graphs only; no held-out-family protocol, so zero-day claims don't transfer.

## Its place in our work

Our windowed host graphs are the middle ground the two papers define: order *inside* a window gets aggregated away (PIKACHU would object), order *across* windows survives in sequence (EULER would approve). Cited local [16], §2.4.

---

Explain it back — and then the standing question: *EULER and PIKACHU both claim temporal modelling, and you implemented neither. What did each teach you that the other didn't?*
